outcome: Deliver constructive feedback anchored to observable actions and agreed next steps, so the recipient changes their work practice without becoming defensive.
title: Giving Feedback That Changes Behaviour
must_avoid: Numerical assertions without verified source attribution
Learning styles claims or neurolinguistic programming concepts
Fabricated statements presented as genuine historical speech
Opening sequences announcing an agenda such as in this video we will
Abstract conceptual explanations disconnected from a concrete workplace scenario
Shifting across multiple unrelated characters rather than maintaining one running narrative
Trivial recall questions instead of a practical scenario check
Criticising personal character traits or motives rather than specific observable actions
example_posture: A single running workplace scenario featuring a colleague receiving feedback on a concrete project deliverable, carried from initial friction through diagnostic breakdown to a successful revised conversation.

audience.who: Corporate employees who deliver constructive feedback to colleagues or team members
audience.knows: Giving feedback often feels uncomfortable and frequently triggers defensiveness or hurt feelings without correcting the underlying issue
audience.cares_about: Protecting workplace relationships while achieving genuine, lasting improvements in work quality

voice_note: A supportive, experienced colleague offering practical counsel from alongside the viewer. Grounded and calm, avoiding academic lecturing or patronising cheerfulness.
open_questions: Which specific workplace deliverable or scenario best reflects the primary feedback friction points across the organisation
Whether the organisation already adheres to an established feedback framework or terminology that the knowledge sheet should align with
through_line: Effective feedback describes observable actions and mutual future adjustments rather than judging character, turning a confrontation into a shared problem to solve.

must_cover.what: Distinguishing between behaviour change and emotional comfort as the primary objective of constructive feedback
Focusing feedback on observable actions rather than personality traits or assumed intentions
Articulating the concrete operational impact of an action on project outcomes or team performance
Collaboratively establishing concrete next steps and replacement habits instead of unilateral demands
Techniques for de-escalating defensiveness during sensitive corrective conversations

visual_direction: A clean cartoon illustration world showing a person in an everyday office situation, juxtaposing a tense conversation with a collaborative exchange, displaying before and after states, highlighted spoken phrasing changes, and a visible shift from personal tension to a clear forward roadmap.

arc_plan.what: Present a relatable workplace scenario where well-intentioned feedback leaves a colleague feeling defensive and demoralised while repeating the same error on the next deliverable.
Show that separating observable actions from personal interpretation allows feedback to guide concrete changes in work habits while preserving mutual trust.
Contrast vague character critiques with specific behavioural observations to reveal why standard feedback conversations trigger defensive emotional reactions instead of improvement.
Break down the practice of stating objective observations, naming concrete operational impacts, and co-creating a specific replacement habit for the next assignment.
Present a realistic dialogue choice between a subjective character critique and an observation-based action prompt, prompting the viewer to identify which one actually targets behaviour.
Walk through converting an emotionally charged complaint about missed deadlines into a structured behavioural conversation with agreed milestones.
Return to the opening workplace scenario, showing the revised conversation leading to an adjusted workflow, mutual clarity, and an intact working relationship.
